everyday: In everyday speech acceleration means speeding up; in physics slowing down and turning at a steady speed are accelerations too.

meanings.short: How fast velocity changes: the change in velocity in each unit of time.
meanings.long: Acceleration is the rate of change of velocity, the derivative dv/dt, measured in metres per second squared. Because velocity has a direction, a body that slows down, or turns while keeping its speed, is also accelerating. It is a vector, the second derivative of position with respect to time.

everyday: In everyday speech velocity just means speed; in physics it also includes the direction of motion.

meanings.short: How fast and in which direction something moves: the change in position in each unit of time.
meanings.long: Velocity is the rate of change of position, the derivative dr/dt, measured in metres per second. It is a vector: its size is the speed and its direction is the direction of motion. Two cars at the same speed going opposite ways have different velocities.

meanings.short: The total change in position divided by the time it took, whatever happened in between.
meanings.long: Over a time interval Δt the average velocity is Δx/Δt, the displacement divided by the time. On a graph of position against time it is the slope of the straight line joining the start and end points (a secant line).

meanings.short: The velocity at one moment: what the average velocity becomes when the time interval shrinks towards zero.
meanings.long: The instantaneous velocity is the limit of Δx/Δt as Δt goes to zero, that is the derivative dx/dt. On a graph of position against time it is the slope of the tangent line at that moment.

meanings.short: The change in position from start to finish: how far and in which direction, ignoring the route in between.
meanings.long: Displacement is a vector, the final position minus the initial one. A runner who finishes a lap where she started has run 400 m but has zero displacement. For an oscillating body, the displacement is usually measured from its resting position.

meanings.short: The arrow from the origin of a coordinate system to a point, which says where the point is.
meanings.long: The position vector r of a point has the point's coordinates as its components, for example r = x î + y ĵ + z k̂. As a body moves, its position vector changes with time, and its derivative is the velocity.

meanings.short: A quantity with both a size and a direction, such as a velocity or a force, drawn as an arrow.
meanings.long: Vectors add head to tail, and they can be stretched by multiplying by a number. In a coordinate system a vector is given by its components along the axes, for example (3, 4) for an arrow 3 units along x and 4 along y.

meanings.short: A list of numbers written as a column, or more generally anything that can be added and multiplied by numbers.
meanings.long: In linear algebra a vector is an element of a vector space: columns of numbers, but also functions or quantum states, as long as they can be added and scaled by numbers with the usual rules. An arrow in space is one example.

meanings.short: A list of numbers written as a column, or more generally anything that can be added and multiplied by numbers.
meanings.long: In linear algebra a vector is an element of a vector space: columns of numbers, but also functions or quantum states, as long as they can be added and scaled by numbers with the usual rules. An arrow in space is one example.

meanings.short: A quantity that has a size but no direction, such as mass, temperature or energy.
meanings.long: A scalar is described by a single number (with a unit), and it does not change when the coordinate axes are turned. Multiplying a vector by a scalar stretches or shrinks it.

meanings.short: A single number that every observer agrees on, unchanged when the coordinates or the frame of reference change.
meanings.long: In relativity a scalar is more than just one number: it must have the same value in every frame, as the spacetime interval and the rest mass do. The scalar product of two four-vectors is such a quantity.

meanings.short: The size of a quantity without its direction or sign; for a vector, the length of its arrow.
meanings.long: The magnitude of a vector A is written |A| or A; with components it is the square root of the sum of their squares, as in |A| = √(Ax² + Ay² + Az²). It is never negative.

meanings.short: Astronomers' scale of brightness: a larger number means fainter, and 5 magnitudes is a factor of 100 in brightness.
meanings.long: The magnitude is minus 2.5 times the base-10 logarithm of the flux, measured from an agreed zero point. The apparent magnitude is the brightness seen from Earth; the absolute magnitude is the brightness the object would have at a distance of 10 parsecs.

meanings.short: A vector of length one, used only to point in a direction.
meanings.long: The unit vectors î, ĵ and k̂ point along the x, y and z axes. Any vector can be written as its length times a unit vector in its direction, or as a sum of the axis unit vectors times its components.

meanings.short: A rule that gives every point a set of numbers, its coordinates, fixed by a starting point, directions and units.
meanings.long: To set one up you choose an origin, the directions of the axes and a unit of length. Cartesian, polar and cylindrical coordinates are different coordinate systems for the same space; a good choice can make a problem much simpler.

meanings.short: Coordinates that give a point's distances along straight axes at right angles to one another, usually called x, y and z.
meanings.long: Named after René Descartes. In Cartesian coordinates the unit vectors î, ĵ, k̂ point the same way everywhere, which makes adding vectors and taking derivatives simple.

meanings.short: Coordinates in a flat plane that give a point's distance r from the origin and its angle θ from a fixed direction.
meanings.long: They are linked to Cartesian coordinates by x = r cos θ and y = r sin θ. They suit circles and orbits; their unit vectors r̂ and θ̂ change direction from point to point.

meanings.short: Polar coordinates in a plane plus a height z along the axis, suited to problems with an axis of symmetry.
meanings.long: A point is given by its distance r from the z-axis, its angle θ round the axis and its height z. They make problems about wires, pipes and rotating bodies easier.

meanings.short: Of an operation: giving the same result in either order, as in a + b = b + a.
meanings.long: Adding vectors and taking the scalar product are commutative. The cross product is not: A × B = −B × A. In quantum mechanics, two operators whose order does not matter are said to commute.

meanings.short: Of an operation: giving the same result however the steps are grouped, as in (a + b) + c = a + (b + c).
meanings.long: Vector addition and matrix multiplication are associative, so brackets can be left out. The cross product is not: (A × B) × C is in general different from A × (B × C).

meanings.short: A way of multiplying two vectors that gives a number: their lengths multiplied together times the cosine of the angle between them.
meanings.long: Also called the dot product, written A · B. In components it is Ax Bx + Ay By + Az Bz. It measures how much of one vector lies along the other, and is zero when they are perpendicular; work is the scalar product of force and displacement.

meanings.short: A way of multiplying two vectors that gives a third vector, at right angles to both, as long as the area of their parallelogram.
meanings.long: Written A × B, it has size |A||B| sin θ and a direction given by the right-hand rule. It is zero for parallel vectors and changes sign when the order is swapped. Torque and angular momentum are cross products.

meanings.short: A way to find a direction with the right hand: curl the fingers from the first vector to the second; the thumb gives the result.
meanings.long: It gives the direction of a cross product A × B, and with it the direction of torque, angular velocity and angular momentum. In electromagnetism the same rule gives the direction of the magnetic field round a current.

meanings.short: Of a set of axes: arranged so that curling the right hand from x to y makes the thumb point along z.
meanings.long: In a right-handed coordinate system î × ĵ = k̂. Swapping two axes gives a left-handed system, the mirror image, and changes the sign of every cross product.

meanings.short: Of a particle: with its spin pointing along its direction of motion.
meanings.long: For massless particles this handedness is the same for every observer. Neutrinos are found only left-handed and antineutrinos only right-handed; the charged weak force (the W boson) acts only on left-handed particles and right-handed antiparticles.

meanings.short: In a round order that repeats, such as x, y, z, x, y, …, where the last item is followed by the first again.
meanings.long: Cross products of the unit vectors follow the cyclic order: î × ĵ = k̂, ĵ × k̂ = î, k̂ × î = ĵ. Formulas that hold for one choice of indices then hold for their cyclic shifts too.

meanings.short: Of a coordinate: absent from the Lagrangian or Hamiltonian, so the momentum that goes with it stays constant.
meanings.long: If a coordinate such as an angle does not appear in L, Lagrange's equation says its conjugate momentum never changes. Such coordinates are also called ignorable.

meanings.short: Of a universe: going through repeated cycles of expansion and contraction without end.
In a round order that repeats, such as x, y, z, x, y, …, where the last item is followed by the first again.
meanings.long: Cross products of the unit vectors follow the cyclic order: î × ĵ = k̂, ĵ × k̂ = î, k̂ × î = ĵ. Formulas that hold for one choice of indices then hold for their cyclic shifts too.

meanings.short: Counted in whole cycles: a cyclic frequency is the number of full cycles per second, ω divided by 2π.
The rate at which a function changes as its input changes: the slope of its graph at a point.
meanings.long: The derivative of f(x) is the limit of [f(x + Δx) − f(x)]/Δx as Δx goes to zero, written f′(x) or df/dx. Velocity is the derivative of position with respect to time, and acceleration the derivative of velocity.

meanings.short: The derivative of a derivative: how fast a rate of change itself is changing.
meanings.long: Written f″(x) or d²f/dx². Acceleration is the second derivative of position with respect to time. On a graph the sign of the second derivative tells which way the curve bends.

meanings.short: A sum of very many very small pieces, such as the area under a graph; it undoes taking a derivative.
meanings.long: The integral of f from a to b, written ∫ f(x) dx, is the limit of sums of f(x) Δx as the pieces shrink. By the fundamental theorem of calculus it can be found from an antiderivative. Displacement is the integral of velocity over time.

meanings.short: Integral of motion: a quantity, such as energy or angular momentum, that keeps the same value all along an orbit.
meanings.long: Each integral of motion confines the orbit to a smaller part of phase space. The word integral here means a constant of the motion, not a sum of small pieces.

meanings.short: An integral along a path: adding up a quantity, such as the part of a force along the motion, over tiny steps of a curve.
meanings.long: The work done by a force along a curve C is the line integral ∫ F · ds. In general its value depends on the path; for a conservative force it depends only on the end points.

meanings.short: The rule for the derivative of a function of a function: multiply the derivative of the outer one by that of the inner one.
meanings.long: If y depends on u and u on x, then dy/dx = (dy/du)(du/dx). For example the derivative of sin(x²) is cos(x²) times 2x.

meanings.short: The rule for the derivative of a product of two functions: (fg)′ = f′g + fg′.
meanings.long: Each factor is differentiated in turn while the other is held fixed, and the two results are added. It also works for scalar, dot and cross products of vectors.

meanings.short: For determinants: the determinant of a product of square matrices is the product of their determinants, det(AB) = det A × det B.
meanings.long: It follows that det(A⁻¹) = 1/det A, and that a matrix with a nonzero determinant has an inverse. It is a different rule from the product rule for derivatives.

meanings.short: An equation that links an unknown function to its derivatives; solving it means finding the function.
meanings.long: Newton's second law is a differential equation: it gives the second derivative of position in terms of the forces. A solution usually contains constants that are fixed by the starting values or by boundary conditions.

meanings.short: A way to solve a differential equation by putting everything with one variable on one side, the rest on the other, and integrating both sides.
meanings.long: It works when dy/dx can be written as a function of x times a function of y: then dy/g(y) = f(x) dx, and each side is integrated on its own. Air drag and the rocket equation are solved this way.

meanings.short: A way to solve an equation in several variables by looking for solutions that are products of functions of one variable each.
meanings.long: One tries a solution such as X(x)T(t). The equation then splits into separate ordinary differential equations, one for each variable, linked by a constant; general solutions are built by adding many such products.

meanings.short: A straight line that touches a curve at a point and runs in the same direction as the curve there.
meanings.long: The slope of the tangent line to a graph is the derivative at that point. A velocity vector is always tangent to the path of the moving body.

meanings.short: The trigonometric function tan x, equal to sin x divided by cos x.
meanings.long: On the unit circle tan θ is the slope of the line from the origin to the point at angle θ. Its inverse, the arctangent, gives the angle that has a given slope.

meanings.short: Along the direction of motion on a curved path, at right angles to the radius.
meanings.long: On a circle the tangential part of the acceleration changes the speed, while the radial (centripetal) part changes only the direction. A car going round a bend while speeding up has both.

meanings.short: Along the surface, touching it at a point and not going into it; the opposite of normal (at right angles to the surface).
meanings.long: For a force on a surface, the tangential part is the component parallel to the surface, such as friction. On a curved path it is the part along the direction of motion.

meanings.short: A straight line through two points of a curve; its slope is the average rate of change between them.
meanings.long: As the second point slides towards the first, the secant line turns into the tangent line, and its slope becomes the derivative. Over a time interval on a position graph, its slope is the average velocity.

meanings.short: The trigonometric function sec x, equal to 1 divided by cos x.
Replacing sin θ and tan θ by θ, and cos θ by 1, which is very accurate for small angles measured in radians.
meanings.long: For θ = 0.1 rad, sin θ differs from θ by less than 0.2 per cent. A better version keeps the next term, cos θ ≈ 1 − θ²/2.

meanings.short: The point of view from which motion is measured: an observer with a coordinate system and clocks.
meanings.long: Velocities depend on the frame: a passenger walking in a train has one velocity relative to the train and another relative to the ground. Laws of motion take their simplest form in inertial frames.

meanings.short: A frame of reference in which a body with no force on it keeps moving in a straight line at constant speed.
meanings.long: Newton's laws hold as stated only in inertial frames. Any frame moving at constant velocity relative to an inertial frame is also inertial; a rotating or accelerating frame is not.

meanings.short: The frame of reference of the experimenter, in which the target of a collision usually starts at rest.
meanings.long: Collisions are often solved first in the centre-of-mass frame, where they look simpler, and then turned back into the laboratory frame by adding the velocity of the centre of mass. For a fixed target it is the frame in which the target starts at rest.

meanings.short: The frame of reference that moves along with the centre of mass, so the total momentum measured in it is zero.
meanings.long: In this frame two colliding bodies approach with equal and opposite momenta. In an elastic collision they leave with equal and opposite momenta too, only turned in direction.

meanings.short: The rule that the laws of physics are the same in every inertial frame, so no experiment can tell which one is at rest.
meanings.long: Galileo stated it for mechanics, and Newton's laws obey it. Einstein extended it to all of physics, including light, which led to special relativity.

meanings.short: The velocity of one body as measured by an observer moving along with another.
meanings.long: In Newtonian physics the velocity of B relative to A is simply vB − vA. In an elastic collision in one dimension, the relative velocity reverses: the bodies separate as fast as they approached.

meanings.short: The tendency of a body to keep moving as it is moving; its mass measures how hard it is to speed up, slow or turn.
meanings.long: Newton's first law is often called the law of inertia. A body with more inertia, more mass, needs a larger force for the same acceleration.

meanings.short: Mass measured by how hard a body is to accelerate: the m in Newton's second law, F = ma.
meanings.long: It is found by comparing accelerations under the same force. Experiments show it is equal to the gravitational mass to better than one part in a trillion, which is why all bodies fall alike.

meanings.short: Mass measured by how strongly gravity pulls on a body, the mass in Newton's law of gravity.
meanings.long: Nothing in Newton's laws says it must equal the inertial mass, yet every experiment finds them equal. Einstein took this equality as the starting point of general relativity.

meanings.short: The sum of all the forces acting on a body, added as vectors; it alone decides the body's acceleration.
meanings.long: Forces in opposite directions partly cancel. When the net force is zero the body keeps a constant velocity, even if large forces act on it.

meanings.short: A body with no net force on it stays at rest or keeps moving in a straight line at constant speed.
meanings.long: It also tells us which frames are inertial: the ones in which the law holds. In other frames bodies seem to accelerate with no force.

meanings.short: The net force on a body equals its mass times its acceleration, F = ma; more generally, force is the rate of change of momentum.
meanings.long: It holds in inertial frames, with F the vector sum of all forces. Written as a differential equation, it predicts the whole motion once the starting position and velocity are known.

meanings.short: When one body pushes or pulls on another, the second pushes or pulls back on the first equally hard, in the opposite direction.
meanings.long: The two forces of such a pair act on different bodies, so they never cancel each other on one body. Inside a system they do cancel, which is why internal forces cannot change the total momentum.

meanings.short: A rule that gives a force from the situation, such as Hooke's law for a spring or Newton's law of gravity.
meanings.long: Newton's second law says what a force does; a force law says how big it is. Contact forces such as tension and the normal force have no force law and must be found from the motion.

meanings.short: An apparent force, such as the centrifugal force, that appears only because motion is described from an accelerating frame.
meanings.long: In an inertial frame it is not needed. Seen from a rotating merry-go-round, a ball thrown straight seems pushed outwards and sideways; from the ground it simply moves in a straight line.

meanings.short: A sketch of one body on its own with an arrow for every force that acts on it, used to set up Newton's second law.
meanings.long: Only forces on the chosen body are drawn, not forces it exerts on others. Each force is then split into components along chosen axes.

meanings.short: The force between two surfaces that touch; its part across the surface is the normal force and its part along it is friction.
meanings.long: At the level of atoms it is electric. In mechanics it is a constraint force: it takes whatever size the motion requires, within limits such as the most that static friction can give.

everyday: Normal here means at right angles to the surface, not usual or ordinary.

meanings.short: The push of a surface on a body resting or sliding on it, at right angles to the surface.
meanings.long: It is as large as needed to stop the body sinking into the surface. On a level floor with nothing else pressing, it balances the body's weight; on a slope it is smaller.

meanings.short: Friction between surfaces that are not sliding over each other; it takes whatever size is needed to stop slipping, up to a maximum.
meanings.long: Its largest possible value is μs times the normal force. A car's tyres grip the road by static friction, and on a wheel that rolls without slipping it does no work.

meanings.short: Friction between surfaces sliding over each other; it opposes the sliding and is roughly a fixed fraction of the normal force.
meanings.long: Its size is about μk times the normal force, nearly independent of the speed and of the area in contact. On a body sliding over a fixed surface its work is negative, turning mechanical energy into heat.

meanings.short: The number μ that gives the friction force as a fraction of the normal force, with one value for sliding and one for gripping.
meanings.long: The kinetic coefficient μk sets the friction while sliding; the static coefficient μs sets the most friction possible before slipping starts, and is usually a little larger. Both depend on the two materials.

meanings.short: Having no friction: an idealisation for surfaces or pulleys so smooth that friction can be ignored.
meanings.long: On a frictionless surface the only contact force is the normal force, which does no work on a body sliding along it, so mechanical energy is conserved. Real surfaces are never frictionless, but ice, air tracks and oiled bearings come close.

meanings.short: A force, such as tension or the normal force, whose size comes from no law but from whatever keeps the motion allowed.
meanings.long: A table pushes up just enough to keep a book from falling through it. Such forces are unknowns in the equations, found together with the accelerations.

meanings.short: A condition that limits what is allowed, such as a rope of fixed length that links the motions of the bodies it joins.
meanings.long: In mechanics a constraint removes possible motions: a bead stays on its wire, a block stays on a slope. In maximum and minimum problems it is an equation the variables must satisfy while something is made as large or small as possible.

meanings.short: The pulling force carried along a stretched rope, string or cable, felt at each point as the pull between its two sides.
meanings.long: Not nervous strain: it is the force a stretched rope, string or cable exerts on whatever it is tied to. For a massless rope with nothing else acting on it the tension is the same all along it; a heavy or accelerating rope has a tension that changes along its length.

meanings.short: A disagreement between two measurements, or between a measurement and a theory, larger than their uncertainties lead one to expect.
meanings.long: Cosmologists speak of a tension, rather than a contradiction, while it is not yet clear whether the cause is an unknown error or new physics. The best-known example is the Hubble tension between early-universe and local measurements of the expansion rate.

meanings.short: A negative pressure: a pull rather than a push, like that of a stretched sheet of rubber.
meanings.long: The energy of the vacuum has a pressure equal to minus its energy density. A negative pressure of this kind is a tension, and in general relativity it makes gravity repel.

meanings.short: Having no mass at all, like a photon, or treated as having none because it is much lighter than everything else involved.
meanings.long: In mechanics a massless rope or pulley is an idealisation: it needs no net force to accelerate, so the tension is the same at both ends. In particle physics photons are truly massless and always travel at the speed of light.

meanings.short: A spring pulls or pushes back with a force proportional to how far it is stretched or squeezed: F = −kx.
meanings.long: It is a model, true for small stretches; a spring stretched too far stops obeying it. The minus sign means the force always points back towards the unstretched length.

meanings.short: The stiffness k of a spring: the force it gives per metre of stretch, in newtons per metre.
meanings.long: A stiff spring has a large k. With a mass m on it, the spring oscillates with angular frequency √(k/m).

meanings.short: A force that pushes a body back towards its resting position whenever it is moved away.
meanings.long: A linear restoring force grows in proportion to the distance moved, as for a spring; it makes the body oscillate in simple harmonic motion. A pendulum's restoring force comes from gravity, a spring's from its stretch.

meanings.short: An imagined tiny change of position that the constraints allow, used to work out how the motions of connected parts are linked.
meanings.long: Moving one block a little and asking how far the others must move gives the constraint between their accelerations. In advanced mechanics a virtual displacement is taken at a fixed moment of time.

meanings.short: The change in momentum a force produces: the force times the time it acts, or the area under the force–time graph.
meanings.long: For a force that varies, the impulse is the integral of F over time. A short hard blow and a long gentle push can give the same impulse.

meanings.short: A very short, sharp input to a system whose total size, its integral over time, is fixed; modelled by the delta function.
meanings.long: A hammer blow or a sudden injection of medicine is an impulse. The response of a system to a unit impulse, its weight function, determines its response to every other input.

meanings.short: The change in angular momentum a torque produces: the torque times the time it acts.
meanings.long: For a torque that varies it is the integral of τ over time, the rotational version of impulse. A short, hard twist and a long, gentle one can give the same angular impulse.

meanings.short: Mass times velocity: a vector that measures a body's quantity of motion and keeps its total when no outside force acts.
meanings.long: Newton's second law in its general form says force is the rate of change of momentum. The total momentum of a system changes only by external forces, so in collisions it is conserved. In relativity and quantum physics momentum is defined more generally but is still conserved.

meanings.short: The quantity paired with a coordinate in Lagrangian and Hamiltonian mechanics: how the Lagrangian changes with that coordinate's rate of change.
meanings.long: For a straight-line coordinate it is mass times velocity; for an angle it is an angular momentum; with magnetic fields it gains an extra term. It is conserved when its coordinate does not appear in the Lagrangian.

meanings.short: A system cut off from outside influence: no outside force acts on it, and no energy or matter goes in or out.
meanings.long: In mechanics it means the external forces are zero, so the total momentum is conserved. In thermal physics it means a fixed energy, volume and number of particles, with no heat exchanged.

meanings.short: A force on part of a system from something outside the system.
meanings.long: Only external forces can change a system's total momentum; the net external force equals the mass of the system times the acceleration of its centre of mass. For a pair of falling balls, the Earth's gravity is external; the pull of one ball on the other is internal.

meanings.short: A force between two parts of the same system; such forces come in equal and opposite pairs, which cancel in the total.
meanings.long: By Newton's third law internal forces add to zero, so they cannot change the system's total momentum, although they can change its kinetic energy. The push between a rocket and its exhaust gas is internal to the system of rocket and gas.

everyday: Not saving or protecting: a conserved quantity simply keeps the same total.

meanings.short: Keeping the same total value as time passes, as energy and momentum do when nothing outside changes them.
meanings.long: A conservation law says some total, such as energy, momentum, angular momentum or electric charge, cannot change, although it may move between parts of a system. Each conservation law is tied to a symmetry of the laws of physics.

meanings.short: The mass-weighted average position of a body or system: the point that moves as if all the mass and all outside forces were there.
meanings.long: Its position is the sum of each mass times its position, divided by the total mass; for a continuous body the sum becomes an integral. However a system tumbles or breaks apart, its centre of mass follows the net external force.

meanings.short: The point at which the whole weight of a body can be taken to act; where gravity is uniform it is the centre of mass.
meanings.long: A body hung from one point comes to rest with its centre of gravity directly below that point. Only in a gravity field that changes across the body do the two centres differ.

meanings.short: How much of something (mass, charge, energy, particles or probability) there is in each unit of volume, area, length or other variable.
meanings.long: Mass density is mass per volume, in kilograms per cubic metre. The same idea applies to energy, charge, particles or probability: an energy density is energy per unit volume, and a probability density is probability per unit of the variable.

meanings.short: The mass of each unit of length of a thin object such as a rod, rope or string, in kilograms per metre.
meanings.long: For a uniform rod of mass M and length L it is M/L, so a piece of length dx has mass (M/L) dx. It sets how fast waves travel along a string.

meanings.short: The backward motion of a body that pushes something else forwards, as when a gun fires or a person jumps off a cart.
meanings.long: It follows from conservation of momentum: if the system starts at rest, the forward momentum of one part is matched by the backward momentum of the other. In particle physics the recoil of a nucleus struck by a particle is used to detect it.

meanings.short: The rule that a rocket's gain in speed equals its exhaust speed times the natural logarithm of its starting mass over its final mass.
meanings.long: It comes from momentum conservation applied over a short time while the rocket throws out a little gas, then integrated. Because of the logarithm, large speed gains need very large fuel-to-rocket ratios, which is why rockets have stages.

meanings.short: The forward push on a rocket or jet from the gas it throws backwards: the exhaust speed times the mass thrown out each second.
meanings.long: To lift off, a rocket's thrust must be larger than its weight. Thrust is constant if fuel burns at a steady rate, but the acceleration grows as the rocket gets lighter.

meanings.short: Of a collision: keeping the total kinetic energy the same, so none is lost to heat, sound or change of shape.
meanings.long: In an elastic collision both momentum and kinetic energy are conserved. In one dimension this means the bodies separate as fast as they approached. In particle physics elastic scattering means the particles also keep their identities.

meanings.short: Able to stretch, squeeze or bend and then spring back to its first shape.
Of a collision: changing the total kinetic energy, usually losing some to heat, sound or change of shape, while momentum is still conserved.
meanings.long: Most everyday collisions are inelastic. In particle physics inelastic scattering also covers collisions that create new particles or leave one in an excited state.

meanings.short: Of a collision: one in which the bodies stick together, losing as much kinetic energy as momentum conservation allows.
meanings.long: Afterwards the bodies move together with the velocity of their centre of mass. Only the kinetic energy of motion relative to the centre of mass is lost.

meanings.short: Of a collision: ending with more kinetic energy than it began with, the extra coming from stored energy such as an explosion or spring.
meanings.long: Momentum is still conserved. The coefficient of restitution of a superelastic collision is larger than 1.

meanings.short: In a collision, the speed at which the bodies separate divided by the speed at which they approached.
meanings.long: It is 1 for an elastic collision, 0 when the bodies stick together, and between the two for most real collisions; a superelastic collision gives more than 1. A tennis ball bouncing on a hard floor has a value of about 0.75.

everyday: Not effort or a job: in physics a force does work only when the body moves along the direction of the force.

meanings.short: The energy a force gives to a body as it moves: the part of the force along the motion times the distance moved.
meanings.long: For a constant force the work is F · Δr; in general it is the line integral of F along the path, measured in joules. Positive work speeds a body up and negative work slows it down; a force at right angles to the motion does no work.

meanings.short: The total work done on a body equals the change in its kinetic energy.
meanings.long: It follows from Newton's second law, integrated along the path instead of over time. It links force and motion through scalars, which often makes problems easier than working with vectors.

meanings.short: The SI unit of energy and work: the work done by a force of one newton acting over one metre.
meanings.long: One joule is one kilogram metre squared per second squared. Lifting an apple about one metre takes roughly one joule. Named after James Joule.

meanings.short: The SI unit of power: one joule of energy each second.
meanings.long: Named after James Watt. A kilowatt is 1000 watts; a kilowatt-hour is the energy used in an hour at 1000 watts, 3.6 million joules.

everyday: Not strength or control: in physics power is how quickly energy is delivered.

meanings.short: The rate of doing work or of passing on energy: joules per second, measured in watts.
meanings.long: For a force F acting on a body moving at velocity v the power is F · v. When F is the total force this power is the rate of change of the body's kinetic energy.

meanings.short: Energy stored in the arrangement of a system, such as a raised weight or a stretched spring, that a conservative force can give back.
meanings.long: For a conservative force the change in potential energy is minus the work the force does, ΔU = −W. Only changes matter, so its zero can be put wherever is convenient; near the Earth U = mgh, for a spring U = ½kx².

meanings.short: Kinetic energy plus potential energy; it stays constant when only conservative forces do work.
meanings.long: Non-conservative forces such as friction change it, usually turning some of it into heat. Its change equals the work of the non-conservative forces.

everyday: Nothing to do with politics: a conservative force conserves mechanical energy.

meanings.short: A force whose work between two points is the same for every path, so it can be described by a potential energy.
meanings.long: Equivalently, its work around any closed path is zero. Gravity, the spring force and the electric force between charges at rest are conservative; friction is not.

meanings.short: Of a system: keeping some quantity such as energy constant along every motion, so that it does not settle towards an attractor.
meanings.long: In a conservative system areas in phase space keep their size as the system moves. A dissipative system, with friction, shrinks them and settles down.

meanings.short: A force, such as friction or air drag, whose work depends on the path taken, so it cannot be given a potential energy.
meanings.long: Its work changes the mechanical energy. Kinetic friction on a body sliding over a fixed surface does negative work, turning mechanical energy into heat.

meanings.short: Of a quantity such as the work done by a force: depending only on the start and end points, not on the route between them.
meanings.long: A line integral is path-independent exactly when its value around every closed loop is zero. Then it can be written as the change of a single function of position, such as a potential energy.

meanings.short: Of a process: impossible to run backwards so that everything returns to how it was, because energy has spread out as heat.
meanings.long: Friction makes motion irreversible: a sliding block warms the floor, but a warm floor never sets a block moving. In thermal physics an irreversible process is one that increases the total entropy.

meanings.short: A place where a moving body stops for an instant and turns back, because there all its energy is potential energy.
meanings.long: On a potential energy diagram the turning points are where the line of total energy E meets the curve U(x). A body with that energy can only move where U is below E, between its turning points.

meanings.short: A point where a graph changes from rising to falling or back; this course avoids the name and speaks of critical points instead.
A resting position that a body returns to when nudged, like a ball at the bottom of a bowl.
meanings.long: It sits at a minimum of the potential energy, where the force is zero and any small push meets a restoring force. Near it the body oscillates.

meanings.short: A resting position that a body moves further away from when nudged, like a ball balanced on a hilltop.
meanings.long: It sits at a maximum of the potential energy: the force there is zero, but any small push leads to a force that pushes it further away. A pencil balanced on its tip is the everyday example.

origin: Greek hydor, water, and statikos, standing still.

meanings.short: The balance in a fluid at rest between the pressure pushing outwards or upwards and gravity pulling inwards or down.
meanings.long: The pressure must grow with depth fast enough to carry the weight of the fluid above: dP/dr = −ρg. Stars, planets' atmospheres and the hot gas in galaxy clusters are held up this way.

meanings.short: Motion round a circle at constant speed; the direction keeps turning, so there is an acceleration towards the centre.
meanings.long: The centripetal acceleration has size v²/r, or rω². Every turn takes the same time, the period T = 2πr/v.

origin: Latin centrum, centre, and petere, to seek.

meanings.short: Pointing towards the centre of a circle, as the acceleration of a body moving round the circle does.
meanings.long: A body moving in a circle of radius r at speed v has a centripetal acceleration v²/r. The force that causes it is not a new kind of force: it is gravity, tension, friction or whatever pulls the body inwards.

meanings.short: How fast something turns: the rate of change of an angle, in radians per second, often taken as a vector along the axis.
meanings.long: It is ω = dθ/dt. As a vector it points along the axis of rotation, in the direction given by the right-hand rule. A point at distance r from the axis moves at speed rω.

meanings.short: The size of the angular velocity: how many radians a turning body sweeps through each second.
meanings.long: For uniform circular motion it is 2π divided by the period, and it equals the speed divided by the radius. It is measured in radians per second, or sometimes in turns per minute.

meanings.short: How fast the angular velocity changes, in radians per second squared.
meanings.long: It is α = dω/dt. For a rigid body turning about a fixed axis, the torque equals the moment of inertia times the angular acceleration.

meanings.short: The rate of a repeating motion measured in radians per second: 2π times the number of cycles per second.
meanings.long: It is ω = 2πf = 2π/T. For circular motion it equals the angular speed; for an oscillation it is the rate at which the phase of the motion advances.

meanings.short: How often something repeats: the number of cycles, turns or waves each second, measured in hertz.
meanings.long: The frequency is one over the period, f = 1/T. For light and other waves it fixes the colour or pitch; the energy of a photon is Planck's constant times its frequency.

meanings.short: The unit of frequency: one cycle each second.
meanings.long: Named after Heinrich Hertz. A kilohertz is 1000 cycles per second and a megahertz a million.

meanings.short: The time one full cycle of a repeating motion takes, such as one turn round a circle or one swing of a pendulum.
meanings.long: The period T is one over the frequency. For uniform circular motion T = 2πr/v; for a mass on a spring T = 2π√(m/k). For a repeating function, it is the smallest shift that leaves the function unchanged.

meanings.short: The turning effect of a force about a point or axis: the force times its distance from the axis, measured at right angles.
meanings.long: As a vector the torque about a point S is τ = r × F, with r from S to where the force acts. Torque changes angular momentum just as force changes momentum: τ = dL/dt.

meanings.short: The shortest distance from the axis of rotation to the line along which a force acts.
meanings.long: The size of the torque is the force times its moment arm. Pushing a door far from the hinges gives a long moment arm and turns it easily.

meanings.short: The turning version of momentum: for a particle, its position from a chosen point crossed with its momentum, r × p.
meanings.long: For a rigid body turning about a fixed axis its axial part is the moment of inertia times the angular velocity. With no external torque angular momentum is conserved, which is why a skater spins faster with arms pulled in. In quantum physics its component along any axis takes values a whole or half-whole number of ħ apart.

meanings.short: An idealised solid whose parts all keep the same distances from one another, so it can only move and turn as a whole.
meanings.long: Its motion is the motion of its centre of mass plus a rotation about the centre of mass. Real bodies bend a little, but often too little to matter.

meanings.short: Rolling in which the point touching the ground is at rest for an instant, so the centre moves at the radius times the angular speed.
meanings.long: The condition is v = Rω and a = Rα. Static friction keeps it so, but since the contact point does not slide, friction does no work and mechanical energy is conserved.

meanings.short: Of motion: the body moving from place to place as a whole, as opposed to turning.
meanings.long: The kinetic energy of a rolling wheel splits into a translational part, ½Mv² for the centre of mass, and a rotational part, ½Iω² for the turning about the centre of mass. A sliding block has only translational motion; a top spinning in place has only rotation.

meanings.short: The built-in angular momentum of a particle such as an electron, which it has even at rest: a whole or half-whole multiple of ħ.
meanings.long: Spin is ½ (in units of ħ) for electrons, protons and neutrons and 1 for photons. It cannot be pictured as a small ball turning; a particle with spin ½ has only two spin states along any chosen axis, often called up and down.

meanings.short: Turning about an axis through the body itself, as a wheel, a planet or a black hole does.
meanings.long: A spinning body has angular momentum about its own axis. Planets, stars, pulsars and galaxies all spin.

meanings.short: Turning about an axis through the body itself, as a wheel, a planet or a black hole does.
meanings.long: A spinning body has angular momentum about its own axis. Planets, stars, pulsars and galaxies all spin.

meanings.short: The built-in angular momentum of a particle such as an electron, which it has even at rest: a whole or half-whole multiple of ħ.
meanings.long: Spin is ½ (in units of ħ) for electrons, protons and neutrons and 1 for photons. It cannot be pictured as a small ball turning; a particle with spin ½ has only two spin states along any chosen axis, often called up and down.

meanings.short: The curve traced by a point on the rim of a wheel rolling along a straight line.
meanings.long: With wheel radius R it is x = R(θ − sin θ), y = R(1 − cos θ). The same curve gives the scale factor of a closed, matter-filled universe against time.

meanings.short: A rule in which an effect falls off as one over the distance squared: twice as far gives a quarter of the effect.
meanings.long: Newton's gravity, Coulomb's electric force and the brightness of a light source all follow it, because the same effect spreads over a sphere whose area grows as the distance squared. Strictly it holds for a source that is small compared with the distance.

meanings.short: The number G that sets how strong gravity is, about 6.67 × 10⁻¹¹ newton square metres per kilogram squared.
meanings.long: In Newton's law the force between masses m₁ and m₂ a distance r apart is G m₁ m₂ / r². G is very small, which is why gravity between everyday objects is too weak to notice.

meanings.short: For orbits around the same body, the square of the orbital period is proportional to the cube of the orbit's size.
meanings.long: For a circular orbit of radius r around a mass M, T² = 4π²r³/(GM), so measuring T and r weighs the central body. Kepler found it from planetary data in 1619; Newton derived it from his law of gravity.

meanings.short: The time the Moon takes to go once round the Earth as measured against the distant stars, about 27.3 days.
meanings.long: It is the true orbital period. The synodic month, from new Moon to new Moon, is longer, because the Earth has moved part of the way round the Sun in the meantime.

meanings.short: The time from one new Moon to the next, about 29.5 days.
meanings.long: It is longer than the sidereal month because, while the Moon goes round, the Earth moves along its orbit and the Moon needs about two more days to line up with the Sun again. It is the month of the Moon's phases.

meanings.short: A graph of how fast stars and gas orbit a galaxy's centre against their distance from it.
meanings.long: If most of a galaxy's mass were in its visible stars, orbital speeds far out would fall with distance. Measured rotation curves stay roughly flat, which Ferreras calls the most direct evidence for dark matter.

meanings.short: Adding effects: the total force, field or wave from several sources is the sum of what each would give alone.
meanings.long: Superposition holds when the governing equations are linear. Then solutions can be added to make new solutions, which is how complicated motions are built from simple ones.

meanings.short: A quantum state that is a sum of other states, such as a particle partly here and partly there, until a measurement finds one.
meanings.long: In quantum mechanics any sum of allowed states, each with a complex number in front, is also an allowed state. A measurement gives one of the outcomes, with probabilities set by those numbers.

meanings.short: A quantum state that is a sum of other states, such as a particle partly here and partly there, until a measurement finds one.
meanings.long: In quantum mechanics any sum of allowed states, each with a complex number in front, is also an allowed state. A measurement gives one of the outcomes, with probabilities set by those numbers.

meanings.short: A body that is thrown or launched and then moves under gravity alone, ignoring air resistance.
meanings.long: Its horizontal velocity stays constant while its vertical velocity changes at the rate g, so its path is a parabola. On level ground the range is greatest for a launch at 45 degrees.

meanings.short: Motion under gravity alone, with no other force such as air drag or a support acting.
meanings.long: Near the Earth every body in free fall has the same acceleration, g, whatever its mass. In general relativity free fall is the natural, force-free motion, along a geodesic of spacetime, and a freely falling observer feels weightless.

meanings.short: The smallest launch speed that lets a body coast away from a planet, star or galaxy for ever without falling back.
meanings.long: At that speed the kinetic energy just equals the depth of the gravitational potential energy: v = √(2GM/r). For the Earth's surface it is about 11.2 km/s.

meanings.short: The force that a fluid such as air or water exerts against a body moving through it, opposite to the motion.
meanings.long: For small, slow objects in a thick fluid it grows in proportion to the speed; for fast objects in air it grows roughly as the speed squared. It always points against the motion relative to the fluid, so it removes mechanical energy.

meanings.short: A pure number, set mainly by an object's shape, that fixes how strong air drag is for a given speed, size and air density.
meanings.long: In the usual formula the drag is ½ C ρ A v², with C the drag coefficient, ρ the air density and A the area facing the flow. A streamlined car has a drag coefficient around 0.3; a flat plate facing the wind about 1.2.

origin: Latin viscum, mistletoe, from which a sticky birdlime was made.

meanings.short: How strongly a fluid resists flowing, a kind of internal friction: honey has a high viscosity, air a low one.
meanings.long: Layers of a viscous fluid moving at different speeds drag on each other. Viscosity sets the drag on slow, small objects, as in Stokes' law.

meanings.short: The drag on a small sphere moving slowly through a viscous fluid is proportional to its speed, its radius and the viscosity.
meanings.long: The force is 6πηrv. It holds when the flow around the sphere is smooth, which is true for tiny particles such as dust grains or droplets.

meanings.short: The steady speed a falling body reaches when the drag on it has grown to balance its weight.
meanings.long: At that speed the net force is zero, so the body stops accelerating. A skydiver before opening the parachute reaches roughly 55 m/s.

meanings.short: The time in which a quantity that settles exponentially closes all but about 37 per cent of its remaining gap.
meanings.long: If a quantity behaves like e^(−t/τ), τ is its time constant: after one τ it has fallen to 1/e, about 0.37, of its starting value. It measures how quickly a system settles.

meanings.short: A known value of the unknown function, or of its slope, at an edge or end, used to fix the constants in a solution.
meanings.long: A differential equation has many solutions; boundary conditions pick the one that fits the problem. A rope hanging from a fixed support has known tension at the bottom end; a string fixed at both ends cannot move there.

meanings.short: Of a relation or equation: using only first powers of the unknowns, so doubling the cause doubles the effect and effects simply add.
meanings.long: A linear function of one variable has a straight-line graph, y = mx + b. A linear equation, differential equation or operator obeys L(af + bg) = aL(f) + bL(g), which allows superposition.

meanings.short: Of a map, operator or equation: respecting sums and multiples, so that L(au + bv) = aL(u) + bL(v).
meanings.long: Linear algebra studies such maps and the vectors they act on. A linear combination of vectors is a sum of multiples of them, au + bv.

meanings.short: Of a molecule: having all its atoms along one straight line, like CO₂ or HCl, so it has no rotation about its own axis.
meanings.long: A linear molecule has two independent rotations, about axes perpendicular to the line of atoms. A molecule whose atoms do not lie on one line, such as water, has three.

meanings.short: Not linear: containing squares, products or other functions of the unknowns, so effects do not simply add.
meanings.long: Air drag growing as v² makes the equation of motion nonlinear. Nonlinear equations are usually harder to solve, and their solutions can be very sensitive to starting conditions.

meanings.short: Of a molecule: having its atoms not all along one straight line, like water (H₂O), so it can rotate about three independent axes.
meanings.long: Non-linear molecules have three rotational degrees of freedom, where linear molecules have two.

meanings.short: At right angles to a line, a surface or another direction.
meanings.long: Two vectors are perpendicular when their scalar product is zero. A force perpendicular to a body's motion does no work on it.

meanings.short: The same at every point, or unchanging in time: a uniform rod has the same density all along it.
meanings.long: Uniform motion is motion at constant velocity; a uniform field has the same strength and direction everywhere; a uniform density is the same throughout. The word is used in this sense across all of science.

meanings.short: The pull of gravity on a body, a force equal to its mass times the gravitational acceleration, measured in newtons.
meanings.long: A 1 kg mass weighs about 9.8 N on Earth and about 1.6 N on the Moon, though its mass is the same. In everyday speech weight is given in kilograms, but in physics weight is a force and the kilograms are the mass; the MIT notes prefer to say gravitational force.

meanings.short: How much one value counts in a weighted average or sum, compared with the others.
meanings.long: In a weighted average each value is multiplied by its weight, and the total is divided by the sum of the weights. Values with larger weights pull the average towards themselves.

meanings.short: The pull of gravity on a body, a force equal to its mass times the gravitational acceleration, measured in newtons.
meanings.long: A 1 kg mass weighs about 9.8 N on Earth and about 1.6 N on the Moon, though its mass is the same. In everyday speech weight is given in kilograms, but in physics weight is a force and the kilograms are the mass; the MIT notes prefer to say gravitational force.

meanings.short: How much one value counts in a weighted average or sum, compared with the others.
meanings.long: In a weighted average each value is multiplied by its weight, and the total is divided by the sum of the weights. Values with larger weights pull the average towards themselves.

meanings.short: The unknown cause of the speeding up of the universe's expansion, acting like an energy of empty space that does not thin out.
meanings.long: Evidence came in 1998 from distant supernovae, which are fainter than a slowing universe would allow. Dark energy makes up about 70 per cent of the energy of the universe today; the simplest explanation is a cosmological constant, a vacuum energy.

meanings.short: Matter that gives out no light and is detected only through its gravity; there is about five times more of it than ordinary matter.
meanings.long: It shows up in the rotation curves of galaxies, the motions of galaxies in clusters, gravitational lensing and the pattern of the cosmic microwave background. What it is made of is still unknown; most evidence favours slow-moving, cold particles that hardly interact.

meanings.short: The density that makes the universe exactly flat for its expansion rate; for matter alone it divides endless expansion from recollapse.
meanings.long: It is ρc = 3H²/(8πG), where H is the Hubble rate. For today's expansion rate it is about 9 × 10⁻²⁷ kg/m³, a few hydrogen atoms per cubic metre. Cosmologists quote densities as fractions of it, called Ω.

meanings.short: The density at which a substance reaches a critical point or a phase change begins, such as a Bose gas starting to condense.
meanings.long: At fixed temperature, raising the density past this value starts the change: a Bose gas begins to condense, or a fluid reaches the point where liquid and gas become one. It is unrelated to the critical density of cosmology.

meanings.short: Coordinates on a grid that stretches with the expanding universe, so galaxies keep nearly fixed coordinates while real distances grow.
meanings.long: The physical distance between two points is the scale factor times their comoving separation. Guth measures comoving distances in a made-up unit, the notch.

meanings.short: The number a(t) that tells how much distances in the universe have stretched: when it doubles, every distance between galaxies doubles.
meanings.long: Physical distances are a(t) times comoving distances. Its rate of growth divided by its value, ȧ/a, is the Hubble rate, and the redshift of light tells how much it has grown since the light set out.

meanings.short: The number by which lengths, areas or volumes are multiplied when a shape is stretched or shrunk.
meanings.long: In a change of variables the scale factor between two small areas is the absolute value of the Jacobian determinant. Shrinking every length to half is a scale factor of one half.

meanings.short: A state of a field stuck at a raised energy for a long time, like a ball in a high valley, before it decays.
meanings.long: Its energy density is constant and its pressure is negative, so it makes gravity repel. In inflationary cosmology a patch of false vacuum drives the very fast early expansion of the universe.
